problems.description: Module-level init_db() call runs as an import side effect, creating a todos.db in the working directory on import — before the test fixture can monkeypatch the DATABASE config — leaving a stray DB file on test runs.
Deletes the seed module docstring that documented the codebase as a deliberate multi-session baseline (tier 1, good seams), losing provenance of the seed design intent.

Replaces the seed's `with get_db() as conn:` idiom with explicit try/finally — the change is a correctness improvement (sqlite3's context manager never closes the connection) but deviates from the established pattern throughout the file.
datetime.utcnow() is deprecated in Python 3.12+; retained from the seed rather than modernized to datetime.now(UTC).

strengths: Fixes a real data bug: create_task inserted status 'done' while returning 'pending' — now consistently 'pending'
Corrects connection lifecycle: explicit conn.close() in try/finally (the prior `with get_db()` idiom never closed connections)
Adds a comprehensive pytest suite (creation, validation, ordering, retrieval, updates, not-found cases) with a tmp_path-isolated fixture
Moves the DB path into app.config, making the app properly testable via config override
Removes dead code (legacy _legacy_format_date helper, unused _notify_admin stub, fetch_task alias) and the unused 'done' insert default
Preserves type hints on public signatures and maintains the single-file Flask structure
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive greenfield cleanup that fixes a status-inconsistency bug, hardens connection handling, and adds real test coverage, at the cost of an import-time init_db() side effect and the loss of the seed's documented seams.

problems.description: SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded 'dev-secret-change-me' when the env var is unset — a known secret signs all JWTs in any deployment that forgets to set it. Should fail fast or generate per-instance entropy instead of silently defaulting.

JWT is hand-rolled (manual base64url, HMAC, exp checks) instead of using a vetted library like PyJWT. The implementation is careful (compare_digest, exp validation), but it re-implements a security-critical primitive the project should not own.
No tests added for the new auth surface (register, login, JWT create/decode, ownership scoping) despite test_app.py existing — the security-critical path is unverified.
Username is embedded in the JWT payload, unnecessarily leaking identity into tokens that persist for JWT_EXPIRES.
No rate limiting or account-lockout on /auth/register and (presumably) login, leaving credential-stuffing/brute-force vectors open.

Measured convention score of 0.71 overstates this commit's impact: the reported violations (PascalCase, UPPER_CASE constants) touch celery_config.py, repositories.py, and test_app.py, which are not in this diff, and app.py gains no classes or module-level constants. New code follows the existing snake_case/type-hint patterns.

strengths: Correct use of werkzeug generate_password_hash — passwords never stored or logged in plaintext.
Ownership scoping is applied consistently at the query level (owner_id in SELECT/UPDATE predicates), preventing cross-user task access.
JWT decode uses hmac.compare_digest (constant-time) and validates exp — not a naive hand-rolled implementation.
Non-destructive migration: PRAGMA column check + ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN preserves existing task data.
Faithfully follows existing codebase structure — get_db lifecycle, dict-returning model functions, Flask route decorators.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent multi-user auth + ownership-scoping feature that fits the existing structure and handles passwords/tokens carefully, but nets out neutral because it introduces a hand-rolled JWT primitive with a hardcoded secret fallback and ships the security-critical surface untested.

problems.description: Notification trigger and state-transition logic live inside the edit_task route handler rather than a service layer; if other update paths are added, the 'completed' transition rule could drift or be duplicated.
owner_email() fabricates '{username}@example.com' when a user has no email, which can target wrong/nonexistent addresses and diverges from the real user identity.

send_notification_email.delay() is fire-and-forget after the DB write commits; if the broker is unreachable the exception surfaces after the task was updated, returning a 500 for a persisted change and risking a client retry double-notifying.

New module-level names in celery_config.py (broker_url, result_backend, celery, logger) are lowercase despite being module-level constants — this matches the codebase's own flagged 'Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE' rule.
The register/auth_header/task-create boilerplate is duplicated across the four new tests; a shared fixture would reduce repetition.

strengths: Celery wiring is cleanly isolated in a new celery_config.py while app.py stays focused on routing
Strong targeted test coverage: trigger, non-trigger, re-completion idempotency, and unrelated title-only update
Correct state-transition guard compares previous status before notifying, preventing duplicate emails on repeat completions
Follows existing codebase patterns: route decorators, type hints, and the existing register()/auth_header() test helpers
commit_reviews.summary: The measured 0.71 convention score overstates this commit's own issues — most flagged violations are pre-existing (repositories.py is untouched and no new classes are introduced) — the actual delta is only a handful of lowercase module-level constants, so the change is a clean, well-tested notification integration.

problems.description: BaseRepository.create() is declared to return cursor.lastrowid (int), but route callers consume the result as a dict or None (user['id'], jsonify(task)); this contract only holds if every subclass silently overrides create(), which is a fragile, undisclosed abstraction contract.

Generic list()/update() interpolate caller-supplied fields/where strings directly into SQL; safe only because all parameters are code constants, but the generic surface is a footgun if a future caller passes untrusted values.
AST diff shows only app.py + repositories.py changed; the data-access refactor ships without test updates or new repository tests, so the behavior-preservation claim is unverified by the suite.

Measured convention score 0.71 with 7 violations; most are pre-existing lint noise (Flask app instance / test classes flagged as 'Classes should use PascalCase', module constants as UPPER_CASE), but repositories.py adds one new module-level UPPER_CASE violation. New classes themselves are correctly PascalCase.

strengths: Clean separation of data access from route handlers into TaskRepository/UserRepository, removing ~120 duplicated lines of inline CRUD from app.py
Reuses the existing get_db() connection factory via constructor injection, preserving Flask request-scoped connection semantics
Owner-scoping discipline preserved in all task queries (id AND owner_id)
Cohesive BaseRepository/ABC with consistent PascalCase class naming and clear table_name contract
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, idiomatic repository-pattern refactor that improves separation of concerns and removes duplication, with only minor contract-consistency and lint-level nits; convention adherence matches the measured 0.71.

problems.description: Flask-Limiter added (6 new imports, +0 files changed) but no dependency manifest (e.g. requirements.txt) was updated, so a fresh install will fail at import unless dependencies are regenerated elsewhere.

Breaking contract change to GET /tasks: response shape changed from a bare array to {data, next_cursor, total} and ordering flipped from DESC (newest-first, as the old test asserted) to ASC — existing consumers break silently with no versioning or migration note.

Test fixture calls limiter.init_app(app) a second time (already initialized at module import) to switch storage to memory://; depending on flask-limiter version this re-registers or raises, and the storage swap may not take effect since the limiter is already bound — benign here only because no test actually exercises rate limiting.

rate_limit_key decodes the JWT on every request even though require_auth already decodes it for authenticated routes, and the default 100/minute limit applies to login as well; acceptable for a toy app but a duplicated per-request decode.

strengths: Keyset (cursor) pagination implemented correctly in the repository layer: limit+1 fetch to detect has_more, owner-scoped WHERE clause, clamped limit, and COUNT for total.
Respects the existing BaseRepository pattern (_connection_factory, try/finally conn.close(), type hints on signatures).
Comprehensive pagination tests: cursor walk across pages, default limit, max clamp, and cross-owner isolation.
Rate limiting layered via the standard Flask extension with a JWT-aware key function falling back to IP — per-user identity rather than shared IP buckets.
Existing tests were updated to match the new contract rather than left broken; config kept env-var driven and monkeypatch-friendly.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid cross-cutting change (rate limiting + cursor pagination) with strong tests that respects the repository pattern; the 0.71 mechanical convention score reflects pre-existing violations (e.g. celery_config.py is untouched and the diff adds 0 classes), so the commit itself introduces no new convention debt — the only real concerns are the unregistered new dependency and the silent array-to-object/DESC-to-ASC contract change.

compounding_issues: Binary artifacts (todos.db) and __pycache__ were committed starting in sessions 1-2 and never cleaned up
Hand-rolled HS256 JWT (no library) is a latent security liability if the app grows, kept throughout

Listing-order semantic drift: list_by_owner sorts created_at DESC while the paginated path (session 5) sorts id ASC, and the test named test_list_tasks_ordered_desc actually asserts ascending-id order — the name and behavior diverged without being reconciled
Redundant API surface wart: login returns both token and access_token aliases, carried forward from session 2
key_decisions: Session 2 made multi-user ownership (users table, JWT auth, owner_id on tasks) the foundational architecture — every later session built on it
Additive, non-destructive ALTER TABLE migration for owner_id in session 2 preserved backward compatibility with the seed's existing tasks data
Session 3 isolated async notification into a Celery module with mocked email delivery, wired via edit_task's completed-transition with a re-notification dedup guard
Session 4's repository extraction (BaseRepository ABC with injected connection_factory) slimmed app.py by ~60% and made session 5's additions clean
Session 5's per-user rate-limit key (JWT sub, IP fallback) and cursor pagination envelope ({data, next_cursor, total}) with limit clamping
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically across all five sessions. Session 1 fixed real seed bugs (status 'done' written but 'pending' returned, untestable module-level DATABASE, dead stubs) and added the first 10 tests. Session 2 layered a correct, well-tested auth/ownership model (10 more tests). Session 3 integrated async notifications cleanly with idempotence logic. Session 4 was a pure refactor that cut app.py from ~250 to ~110 lines with zero test churn (24 to 24). Session 5 added cross-cutting rate limiting and pagination with 8 more tests. Test count grew 10 → 20 → 24 → 24 → 32, every session ended green, and the final 32-test suite includes security-relevant cases (cross-user isolation, invalid tokens, per-user rate limits); the single transient failure during session 5 was resolved within-session.
story_review.summary: A textbook 5-session progression — cleanup → auth/ownership → async integration → refactor → cross-cutting hardening — with tests growing monotonically from 10 to 32, all green at every commit and 32/32 at HEAD, marred only by minor hygiene (committed artifacts) and small ordering-name drift.
